Cognitive function assessments in Alzheimer's clinical trials are frequently utilizing digit symbol substitution tests, a task whose performance typically adheres to a normal distribution. The rate at which cognitive function declines is influenced by whether participants are receiving the active treatment or placebo, with clinical trials measuring this decline over time to analyze the treatment's effectiveness. However, utilizing standard statistical tests to analyze performance may overlook nuanced patterns that arise. In this study, a novel statistical method is proposed to assess treatment effects across various timepoints simultaneously. By employing natural cubic splines, this approach identifies when and to what extent the active treatment has the most significant impact. Data from 1,014 participants across 11 clinical trials was analyzed to demonstrate that active treatments significantly reduced cognitive function decline between six and thirty-six months into the study. Furthermore, a comprehensive review of existing literature revealed that no other method exists to determine optimal timepoints for evaluating active treatments in clinical trials, a gap that this statistical method successfully addresses.

A novel method for discovering dominant transition routes between two given states in dynamical systems is introduced by a non-local technique that doesn't require explicit computation near singularities. This approach is based on a variational principle that maximizes the action functional for both gradient systems and Hamiltonian systems. As an illustration, we apply this method to determine main transition routes in systems featuring multiple saddle points. Furthermore, we provide mathematical justification for the given algorithm by showing that the action functional is semiconcave in specific contexts, allowing for convergence of global minima sequences. Additionally, we present several examples of transition paths in diverse systems.

This study provides the L^p tomotonic convergence for parabolic complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations with the exponent p approaching infinity, along with the L^∞ norm convergence of the solutions.

In a recently proposed strongly-typed lambda-calculus, all terms are guaranteed to compute functions that belong to specific subclasses of regular functions, that is, predictable, limited types of functions used in computability theory. This development demonstrates the ability to create strongly-typed lambda-calculi for certain restricted classes of regular functions depending on algebraic structures and gives rise to interesting type systems with a limited number of allowed variables in the type definitions.

We establish a strategic approach to express the Stratonovich integral in terms of Ito integrals, specifically when the integrand involves conditional distribution flow functions. This concept finds application in describing how the mean of a random parameter evolves under a mean-field control influence. We provide a concrete example to illustrate this structural relationship in the context of conditional distributions.

Building on previous research, specifically a 2019 paper, the definition of 2-hyperbolic groups with finite standard spaces was introduced, leading to the development of a novel standard framework based on the rough isometry of such groups to ultrametric spaces. In this same context, the rough isometry of a hyperbolic group to an ultrametric space was further explored. As a result, a generalised version of the standard framework was created for hyperbolic groups, encompassing the original framework for 2-hyperbolic groups. A key discovery in this new area is that any hyperbolic group can be roughly isometric to a product of two specific spaces: an ultrametric space and an $(\epsilon, \eta)$-2-hyperbolic space, leading to the conclusion that every hyperbolic group can be approximated with arbitrary precision by a product of a finite group and an abelian group. This approximation process forms the basis of a space product theorem. In the context of discrete groups, the rough isometry of such group products corresponds to the rough isometry of the product of their respective Cayley graphs with finite generating sets, resulting in a novel decomposition theorem that shows the group can be decomposed into a product of two hyperbolic groups, and potentially an extra finite group, again to arbitrary precision. In the particular case where the group is finitely generated, the decomposition involves the product of two 2-hyper

This study introduces the MCT3SD task, an extended version of the standard Text-to-SQL domain called Multi-Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL. The MCT3SD task consists of multiple distinct domains, each with its own database and query language. Unlike traditional text-to-SQL systems, these domains are completely separate and do not share any common language. Each query has its own unique syntax within its respective database schema. Given its novel nature, the task presents significant challenges for both humans and machines. To address these difficulties, the task was designed with two distinct objectives in mind: first, to identify the relevant attributes and values within the database; second, to group attributes according to their semantic relationships. To accomplish these goals, the proposed MCT3SD task is framed as a multi-step generation problem that involves language modeling and graph neural networks. The task is further extended by incorporating an auxiliary task, which enables the model to group attributes within its step-by-step query generation process. The task was created using real-world SQL queries collected from publicly available datasets and features two distinct types of databases: one derived from Wikipedia and another from Amazon product catalogs. The study provides a detailed evaluation of the task's feasibility, the MCT3SD's complexity, and the current state of the art solutions on text-to-SQL systems. The study showcases the efficacy of the multi-domain task's auxiliary task in improving the overall query generation accuracy across different databases.

In this study, a secure navigation framework is proposed for multi-robot systems using a game-theory approach. It addresses challenges such as navigating around obstacles and loss of information due to sensor reading failures. A risk-aware control method is developed to mitigate the risk of failure and ensure secure navigation. By incorporating an evaluation of model uncertainty into the cost function, the control strategy makes decision-making under uncertain model conditions. The risk-sensitive navigation protocol is demonstrated using simulation in both 2D and 3D environments, focusing on obstacle avoidance and sensor failure scenarios.

Recent discoveries of numerous dwarf galaxies within the Andromeda galaxy's sphere of influence have offered valuable insights into the process of reionization.  To better comprehend reionization, it is crucial to identify even fainter reionization-residual galaxies within the sphere of influence.  Focusing on the region near Andromeda's halo, a new galaxy, Andromeda XXV, has been discovered.  Andromeda XXV is an SFG, distinguished by its red color, low surface brightness, and low mass.  Notably, Andromeda XXV's SFR is significantly lower than that of similar galaxies, suggesting an early reionization period.  As the first SFG with a low central dark matter density, Andromeda XXV highlights the necessity of incorporating SFR data into future reionization surveys.

In the context of massive connectivity systems, a crucial challenge involves designing non-orthogonal user sequences for reliable detection amidst severe inter-user interference and channel fading. To address this issue, conventional methods employing orthogonal sequences, which are highly susceptible to interference and unsuitable for grant-free massive connectivity, are inadequate. A novel approach utilizing genetic algorithms to generate user sequences in code and frequency domains is proposed, thereby enabling simultaneous optimization. To facilitate sequence detection, a two-stage algorithm incorporating a machine learning-based classifier is developed, which achieves superior performance compared to conventional detectors. By training a classifier to predict detected user identities and employing a linear filter to minimize the mean square error between the filtered and original received signals in the second stage, this approach achieves enhanced detection performance. Furthermore, a machine learning-based classifier is trained to predict the likelihood of correct user detection, thereby enabling reliable user detection, which is essential for massive connectivity. By incorporating this reliability metric into a classifier-assisted linear filter detector, this approach achieves enhanced detection performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance, thereby validating its potential for massive connectivity.

Several approximate methods have been devised for calculating the thermodynamic properties of gas mixtures, including humid air, to expedite the calculations. However, many of these simplified formulas do not consistently adhere to the fundamental laws of energy conservation and thermodynamic coherence. In this research, we derive accurate equations based on the ideal gas model for key quantities such as specific enthalpy, the specific heat ratio, the speed of sound, and the heat capacity. These ideal gas-based formulas align neatly with the theorems governing specific heat, the speed of sound, and the ratio of specific heat. Moreover, a simplified expression for particular humidity is formulated based on the specific enthalpy equation. We establish the validity of these simplified expressions under various conditions and confirm their consistency with the specific enthalpy theory. Additionally, we show that the sum of the particular humidity and the total water vapor density yields a precise model adhering to thermodynamic coherence principles. These findings also reveal the relationship of the total water vapor density with saturation water vapor density under different temperatures and pressures.

We introduce the concept of outer algebras within the framework of matroid theory, and demonstrate a group theoretic interpretation for this notion, as well as establish essential properties and properties related to symmetry. Additionally, we reveal the systematic structure of these outer algebras within matroids, and identify the conditions under which they exhibit homomorphisms, including a characterization for those homomorphisms when the involved matroids are projective in nature.

In task-oriented dialogue, accurately identifying the user's intent and related information, which forms the dialogue state, is a critical task heavily reliant on precise automatic speech recognition. However, audio inputs often produce ambiguous results, leading to errors in downstream applications. To tackle this issue, we suggest a method for training an uncertainty classifier that analyzes ASK outputs from confusion networks, which in turn guides the dialogue state monitoring process. Experimental results on the MultiWOZ dataset confirm the effectiveness of our approach.
To compute certain stable sheaves on a curve within Sage, we employ the Chaudhri-Katz-Schiffmann Resolving Scheme as an input.

Influence diagrams are powerful decision-making tools that effectively combine decisions, uncertain data, and desired outcomes. They've been used in various fields, including economics, healthcare, and artificial intelligence. This paper delves deeper into the underlying complexity of three major frameworks within influence diagrams, including the Bayesian framework, structured prediction, and decision learning. By exploring their hidden connections, the paper reveals a previously overlooked relationship between them, suggesting that they might be surface-level representations of a unified, more abstract framework. Ultimately, the goal is to create a singular, cohesive entry point for designing influence diagrams that can capture the full spectrum of problems, thereby streamlining research and development in this area.

We introduce a method for measuring entanglement in a two-qubit optical system that achieves the highest possible precision, utilizing single-photon detection only. This technique enables the measurement of entanglement for any photonically encoded two-qubit state through direct probability recordings from optical modes. It can accurately handle real GHZ-like states, exhibiting minimal error in measuring experimentally prepared entanglement, even with relatively low photon number (around 10). This optimal approach is contrasted with standard asymmetry of time reversal (ART) for comparison.

The reduction of anomalous transport in plasma, achieved through the formation of islands within the magnetically confined environment, is an established phenomenon. These isolated regions of improved confinement are referred to as palm tree modes, and they have been detected using neutron scanning cameras by monitoring the neutron emission originating from the edge of the magnetically confined plasma. A detailed study of these isolated regions of improved confinement, focusing on the specific characteristics of the plasma edge, has been conducted via high-resolution laser interferometry and Langmuir probe measurements. This study focuses on the reduction of turbulence and transport in plasma, achieved through the formation of islands within the magnetically confined environment, and the specific characteristics of these isolated regions, known as palm tree modes, in the JET tokamak.

Deep neural networks have become increasingly reliant on vast amounts of data, making it difficult to deploy them in environments with limited resources or high maintenance costs. Continual learning has emerged as a promising solution to mitigate this challenge by enabling models to acquire and retain knowledge across multiple tasks sequentially. Current approaches to continual learning typically employ complex, fine-tuned pre-trained neural networks, and as a result, they are prone to the well-documented problem of catastrophic forgetting. We question the necessity of these elaborate models and their fine-tuning processes. Instead, we propose Neural Structured Histories (NSH), a straightforward baseline that tackles catastrophic forgetting by training a neural network alongside a comprehensive database that stores the flow of information through the network over time. In contrast to previous approaches that rely on graph-based models to capture this flow, NSH utilizes a neural network to learn and store the information graph dynamically, thereby allowing for a more accurate representation of the data's underlying structure. Our experiments demonstrate that NSH outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in continual learning using graph datasets, as well as CIFAR and MNIST datasets, despite being significantly simpler than its competitors. This research suggests that complex, pre-trained models may not be essential for addressing catastrophic forgetting, and that simpler models may be sufficient for continual learning applications.

Our study focuses on creating a machine-based system to identify human instances of hate speech across multiple modalities. A novel, multi-layered framework is introduced to interpret hate speech through multi-modal, band-specific layers, leveraging both semantic and affective features. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in handling MX-Parl's image and sound inputs for the multi-modal challenge, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and achieving record-breaking accuracy at 77.69. Moreover, the framework's ability to incorporate domain-agnostic layers highlights its capacity to provide understandable multi-modal hate speech identification capabilities.

We investigate network structures composed of Type-I neurons, employing percolation analysis to investigate their synchronous behavior. By utilizing a nonlinear response model and considering both Type-I neurons and synapses as entities within a dual network, we and others found that neurons with higher connection degrees exert a dominant influence on network percolation, revealing that spatial structure exists primarily at the neuron level. This supports previous theoretical assumptions regarding syncronous induction, suggesting that spatial topology can indeed exist at the neuron level. However, our results also indicate that spatial topology emerges more pronounced for stronger synaptic connections and inhibitory couplings. Given that such strong synaptic connections are relatively uncommon, these findings suggest that spatial topology may not be a common feature in biological networks. Instead, we propose that a more pronounced type of spatial structure, primarily defined by neurons and their connectivity, exists, which is characteristic of random networks. We also explore how variations in neuron and synapse distributions affect the properties of these networks, including their size and component distribution.

Reverse engineering of bug-prone software is a complex challenge, with the primary goal of pinpointing the root causes of bugs.  Identifying the code segments responsible for bugs is a critical step toward automated bug repair, but it's a problem that remains difficult to tackle.  A novel approach to addressing this issue involves creating antagonistic test cases that expose bugs, allowing for more precise identification of suspect code areas.  By employing this technique, we've achieved more accurate detection of code segments responsible for bugs, consistently achieving top rankings in multiple bug detection benchmarks.  Our findings demonstrate that a complete bug characterization, including its full functionality and associated constraints, is a crucial criterion for evaluating benchmark performance.  Additionally, we've developed and open-sourced an automated method for generating antagonistic test cases that facilitates bug diagnosis in software.

A data spectrum has been proposed as a new tool for a type of quantum communication known as quantum information forwarding with untrusted senders. This tool is defined as the maximum rate at which quantum information can be extracted from a specific quantum state ensemble, which is related to the quantum state's entanglement properties. Research has shown that data spectra can characterize the fundamental limits of entanglement creation in quantum states. In this study, the capability boundaries of the data-spectrum-based quantum information forwarding strategy (GIFC) are being investigated, specifically in terms of one-way distillable entanglement. To achieve this, the researchers derived upper and lower limits for one-way distillable entanglement, along with corresponding protocols for its computation. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that one-way distillable entanglement serves as a reliable measure of quantum information. When compared to another distillation measure, it was found that one-way distillable entanglement provides a broader range of applicability, especially when considering the GIFC strategy.

A new analytical tool has been created to investigate the collision equation-of-state (EOS) by measuring elliptic flow as a function of eccentricity in binary collisions between nuclei of different sizes. By utilizing varied combinations of light and heavy nuclei, significant variations in shape density can be generated, which in turn allows for a detailed investigation of pressure as a function of density. By incorporating this novel approach into existing analyses, constraints on the EOS can be greatly strengthened, yielding more accurate values for incompressibility in the range of 500-600 MeV as observed in such experiments, which is consistent with a stiff EOS required to explain a neutron star mass of 2 M⊙.

Due to the severe health risks and high costs associated with conventional COVID-19 testing methods, alternative, high-throughput testing methods are being developed. This study explores whether enhanced image acoustics testing can accurately detect early-stage COVID-19 patients, and if so, what neural network models can be used to achieve this goal while safeguarding patient privacy through adversarial training techniques. Our research utilized a unique dataset consisting of CT images, audio recordings, and relevant patient information from a hospital in China. Experiments were performed to evaluate different adversarial training strategies in boosting the ability of neural networks to recognize COVID-19 patients, and the results showed that image-based early detection rates could reach up to 90% through adversarial training, surpassing non-trained models significantly. Our study also shed light on the effectiveness of various adversial training techniques and their impact on training efficiency and accuracy.

This research paper explores the potential of using a Graph Neural Network to create a wireless communication transmitter capable of generating high-quality OFDM signals from digital data input. By modeling the GNN as multiple interconnected nodes with signal processing capabilities, the model can effectively learn to transform the original high-dimensional digital data into a distributed spatial pattern. As a result, the GNN can learn a nonlinear mapping that maps the original data to a distributed spatial pattern. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the GNN model can be trained in an unsupervised manner using a novel optimization approach that minimizes the transmission error without needing a reference model. The model also shows that the GNN model can be trained efficiently using only local gradient updates, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of the model. The model also shows that the GNN model can be trained in a distributed manner using only local communication between neighboring nodes, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of the model. The model also shows that the GNN model can be trained in an unsupervised manner using only local data from each node, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of the model. The model also shows that the GNN model can be trained in a decentralized manner using only local data from each node, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of the model.

A Brazilian province, Goias, faces the second-highest average homicide rate per 100,000 people among all its 242 internal administrative regions. To analyze the spatial pattern of violent crimes across the region, researchers applied Bayesian spatial analysis techniques, specifically exploring the conditional autoregressive model. Their findings revealed the presence of clusters in both high and low crime areas, with six and eight distinct groups identified respectively. Notably, cities experiencing high homicide rates comprised predominantly urban and large metropolitan centers. In contrast, areas of low crime were characterized by a mixture of rural and urban regions. These locations often share common attributes such as proximity to large cities and levels of economic development.

This study explores two main concepts: first, how noise and learning rate adaptability in stochastic gradient descent can be jointly maximized, and second, how this findings can be used to create a faster gradient descent method. In typical stochastic gradient descent, noise is used to introduce randomness, but the current approach takes into account noise levels, an issue-by-issue, to potentially decrease the number of calculations before convergence. The approach is rooted in Bayesian linear regression and has been applied in various machine learning fields like speech recognition and reinforcement learning. In standard usage, noise is used as a safeguard to prevent overconfidence, but the authors argue this use is not fully supported by theory, leading to a new definition of noise that doesn't hinder performance. The results show that noise is used inefficiently in standard techniques and suggest a way to minimize this waste, while also providing insights into when gradient descent works well, has issues, or is stable. The findings also open up new avenues for research, including adaptive learning rate methods, into account both noise and learning rate, adaptive step size methods, and error correction methods, adaptive issue convergence checks. The next generation X-ray satellite, IAXO, is set to significantly advance the field of neutrinoless double beta decay research and solar neutrino detection by leveraging a resistive magnet design with high magnetic field strength and high production rates of $^ {7Be}$ and $^{13}N$. The increased sensitivity will substantially improve our ability to explore the solar interior by measuring high-energy time-of-flight delays and neutrino oscillation patterns in relation to matter density variations near the core.

Self-regenerating systems maintain a stable, autonomous existence through an internal mechanism that sustains their existence, and we observe that a new class of sustaining systems, defined by their properties as an open system, exhibits characteristics similar to life. This open self-regenerating class is characterized by a specific, internal energy structure, known as negative entropy, and displays properties such as a defined boundary, a unified perspective, and a directed evolution pattern. These characteristics enable the system to preserve order, adapt and evolve in response to a disordered environment. Notably, a closed self-regenerating system, exemplified by the van der Pol oscillator, differs from its open counterpart, and we use the dissipative structure theory to analyze the emergence of open self-regenerating systems, and we explore their connection to the theoretical framework of life and its mass and energy supply requirements.

The growth of service robots working alongside humans has led to a pressing need for robust grasping techniques that can accommodate diverse objects and positions.  Traditional grasping methods rely on either expensive depth sensors or inaccurate 2D camera images, while also facing challenges in evaluating their effectiveness.  High-fidelity expensive robots or extensive human-led learning approaches present costly and time-consuming alternatives.  In an effort to overcome these obstacles, a novel database, Extensive Dexterous Grasp Network (DexGraspNet), has been developed through simulation.  Utilizing a physics-based simulation and a diverse range of real-world objects, DexGraspNet generates and evaluates numerous Dexterous Grasp configurations paired with accurate success rates.  Our proposed database encompasses 12 objects and over 5 successful and failed instances across 250,003 different DexGraspNet configurations.  This comprehensive dataset is intended to facilitate research in grasping technologies and will be openly accessible for research purposes upon publication.

This article details a novel technique for incorporating motion correction in free-breathing four-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MRI acquisitions. The proposed approach leverages simultaneous respiratory monitoring to capture motion during each acquisition, using navigators in radiofrequency space. These motion mappings are then applied in reverse to align acquisitions in anatomical space before reconstructing them in an image domain using spiral interpolation and shift-and-add techniques. Utilizing this technique, in-phase and reverse-phase DCE-MRI datasets in three dimensions and four dimensions can be reconstructed without compromising image quality. We successfully applied this technique to reconstruct DCE-MMRI datasets in multiple healthy human volunteers, observing superior image quality and sharpness compared to other methods. Moreover, the technique's efficacy was further demonstrated through the evaluation of tumor segmentation in non-small cell lung cancer patients, where we found comparable segmentation results to a free-breathing single scan acquisition. Ultimately, the presented motion correction technique facilitates the creation of high-quality, dose-efficient DCE-MRI acquisitions by integrating multiple acquisitions in three dimensions.

Model compression through knowledge distillation has garnered significant interest, yet previous approaches have led to the loss of crucial temporal dependencies in datasets for smaller, compressed models. As a result, previous methods have primarily been employed in contexts with relatively low dependency levels, limiting their effectiveness in more complex scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we developed InDistill, a novel, end-to-end, convolutional neural network that utilizes data flow-preserving distillation to compress a model while maintaining its temporal dependencies. To implement this, we developed a convLSTM-based small, compressed model and designed an data flow-preserving structure within the convLSTM. Furthermore, we designed a convLSTM-to-convLSTM structure for the larger, teacher model to ensure the teacher and student models exhibit similar temporal dependencies. To our knowledge, InDistill represents the first application of data flow-preserving distillation in deep convLSTMs. Our research demonstrates that the new model achieves superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets in image super-resolution tasks, achieving an average gain of 0.16 dB over existing methods.

To establish a topological equivalence between submersion functions and their linear-like foliations on the plane within specified open sets, we propose criteria based on the C^1 norm of the submersion. This criterion ensures topological similarity and provides a metric for submersion stability under such transformations. Furthermore, sufficient conditions are established for necessary and sufficient criteria regarding the existence of submersion extensions under the C^1 norm, facilitating a practical approach to verification.

Plant communities in arid and semi-arid regions rely on a large seasonal migration of large herbivores that consume vegetation outside the grazing season, a process referred to as non-resident grazing. To understand the role of non-resident grazing, a mathematical model was developed to investigate its impact on vegetation growth, biomass, and the occurrence of vegetation patterns, while taking into account different levels of consumption during the grazing and non-grazing periods, the grazing season's length, and the proportion of the year the herd spends off the range. It was discovered that non-resident grazing, contrary to expectations, promotes higher vegetation growth and stability compared to scenarios where there is no grazing or only grazing during the grazing season, prompting a reevaluation of the characteristics of ecosystems shaped by non-resident herds.

The performance of algorithms like CountSketch when given adaptively adjusted data is examined. A subset of a $p$-dimensional vector's entries are counted from samples that have been drawn at a fixed rate from an unknown distribution, and their results are then summed. A matrix $M$ with random entries modifies these sums to produce adaptively adjusted data matrices $\tilde{\mathbf{X}}$. This study investigates whether these adjusted data matrices retain certain properties of the original data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ under adaptively adjusted settings. Specifically, the research focuses on how well the just-sketch data matrix $\tilde{\mathbf{X}}$ approximates vectors when given adaptively adjusted input. Our results show that $\tilde{\mathbf{X}}$ can accurately approximate a significant number of vectors from a distribution's $k$-sparse support but cannot do so when given $k\log n$-sparse vectors. Additionally, the research investigates the potential benefits of knowing a vector's sparsity in designing these data matrices in advance and highlights the potential advantages of knowing a vector's support size in designing these data matrices in advance.

A newly developed quantum Monte Carlo program called ipie has been created to solve the electronic Schrödinger equation using a auxiliary-field variational Monte Carlo propagation method. This program, which stands for Integrated Piezonuclear Interactions Engine, is built upon ipie-rs, a highly-parallel Monte Carlo framework capable of utilizing CPU and GPU resources efficiently. By combining auxiliary-field Monte Carlo with a variational wave function expressed through a neural network, ipie achieves self-consistency, enabling self-interaction correction and accelerating convergence. In addition, ipie incorporates novel features such as stochastic reconfiguration, a self-consistent energy-dependent propagator, and a self-consistent backflow wave function. Through parallel processing on CPUs and GPUs, ipie demonstrates high performance, achieving speedup factors of up to 10 compared to conventional sequential computing approaches. As a result, ipie offers a highly efficient and flexible tool for quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics simulations, particularly those involving electron correlation and strongly correlated systems.

This study explores the application of quantum key distribution in financial systems compatible with blockchain, culminating in the creation of a quantum-enabled trading platform. By leveraging quantum communication, it achieves two critical objectives: ensuring the authenticity of trades and increasing trading velocity. To validate this concept, we simulate a quantum version of the Prisoner's Dilemma game on the quantum cloud infrastructure of IBM's quantum processor, specifically using their 5-qubit IBMQ Bogota device. Our analysis indicates that quantum trading systems exhibit a higher level of trust compared to classical systems, while boasts a high transaction success rate of approximately 98%.

In network markets, a key question is how to maximize total revenue, known as "income," especially when brokering significantly impacts pricing. Bostock et al.'s (2018) work demonstrated that maximizing income on general networks without brokering effects is an intractable problem, but is efficiently solvable when the market graph is tree-like and brokering effects are ignored. Given the significant role brokering plays in market income, this work explores the impact of brokering on these results. The study proves the following: (1) the existence of a limited number of key intermediaries that, if included in the price-setting strategy, will capture at least three-quarters of the potential maximum income; and (2) for certain types of tree structures, an algorithm exists to fully determine the optimal price-setting approach, resulting in at least 80% of the maximum possible income, and doing so in a time that grows linearly with network size when combined with a previously known efficiency guarantee for non-tree networks.

To make language models deployable outside of a data center, large datasets need to be condensed into a concise prompt that can be learned by a smaller, specialized model. This allows the small model to access the vast knowledge of a large language model in an efficient manner. While prior studies have focused on prompt learning for static datasets, abductive research has shown that context-dependent datasets, specifically those dependent on individual sentences, exist. We tackle this challenge within condensation by developing Planning with Acquired Entity Prompts, a planning-based method to automatically condense sentence-level prompts. This method leverages a knowledge graph to assist in prompt learning from abundant sentence pairs. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach on the ABC dataset, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin on all three evaluation metrics while significantly reducing the amount of text required, with a notable decrease in prompt length.

This study presents a novel, direct approach to proving the differentiability of a $n$-dimensional function, given the differentiability of a $n-1$ dimensional function derived from it, and determines the derived derivative.

Researchers have proposed various behavioral and observational measures to identify social phenomena like vocal entrainment in conversations. On the other hand, a growing number of studies aim to develop computational models that enhance its objective evaluation. In a study, it was discovered that existing models do not adequately account for the dynamic shifts in speakers' entropic properties within conversations. As a result, a new dynamic model was proposed to measure the entropic variations between conversation participants, taking into consideration the evolving context, and was tested on a dataset of conversational interactions. The evaluation of the model's effectiveness was conducted through both automatic and human assessments of the simulated dynamics between conversation participants, and the results indicated that it surpasses existing benchmark models.

A recent study has established a fully symmetric monoidal category which can be seen as a unitary sphere's category of relations, denoted as the lambda-S1-categorical model. This category is characterized by its two fundamental generators and one defining relation. We interpret this structure as a category of quantum manipulations that occur within an unitary sphere environment. This category is not only a group equivalent to the classical S1 group but also a proper category. In this sense, it offers a richer structure than its classical counterpart and can therefore be used to describe quantum processes that cannot be adequately captured by classical group theories. This category serves as a quantum enhancement of the well-known S1 group and provides a framework for understanding complex quantum processes that cannot be adequately described by classical means.

Two specific mathematical findings for the Harper-Bach model's two quasiparticle excitations on a torus have been found. These results were made possible due to a detailed understanding of two key components: the total two-particle wave function and its related current distribution. Building upon these results, further investigations into the quasiclassical descriptions of quasiparticles are suggested for future research. This study also highlights the potential for discovering more accurate mathematical expressions describing multi-quasiparticle excitations within a topological fractional quantum Hall state, which could be a factor in identifying experimentally observable properties of these quasiparticles.

A model of plastic deformation in ice, rooted in viscoplasticity theory, necessitates the use of a non-standard Stokes equations variant, distinguished by its unique mixed boundary conditions and intrinsic constraints, rather than the more conventional coercive variants often explored in the literature. This variant, however, lacks extensive research due to its semicoercive nature, making it particularly challenging to address numerically. We address this gap by proposing a numerical approach that employs Lagrange multipliers to incorporate the constraints directly into the Stokes equations as Lagrange multipliers, thus preserving the problem's original structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by providing finite element methods that achieve optimal convergence rates for both the Lagrange multipliers and velocity fields, achieved through carefully tailored regularity assumptions and discrete inf-sup conditions that are independent of the mesh size.

A survey of star-forming galaxies in a low-redshift cluster, located 200 Mpc away, is presented, utilizing a high-resolution integral field spectrograph. The study focuses on the relationship between galactic properties, star formation, and gas in a cluster environment. The data was analyzed through various metrics, with special attention given to the impact of outflows on star formation. The results indicate that gas-rich galaxies with high star formation rates are responsible for galactic winds, which limit the formation of new stars. The study also reveals that galaxies with wind-driven outflows are less likely to undergo post-wind resumption of these outflows, and instead may experience reduced wind velocities and mass outflow rates, resulting in lower metallicity and molecular gas fractions, and enhanced gas efficiency in star formation.

Our research examines the triangular flow $v_3$ from multiphase transport simulations, specifically for Au+Au and Cu+Collisions at a 7.7 GeV/nucleon incident velocity, revealing that the $v_3$ is highly sensitive to the initial conditions. By comparing the $v_3$ results to experimental data from the PHENIX collaboration, we find that the $v_3$ is in good agreement with actual measurements when assuming that the quark-gluon plasma phase is the first one formed in these collisions, whereas a hadronic phase that forms first would be inconsistent with our findings. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that Au+Au collisions have a greater $v_3$ value than Cu+Cu collisions, which is in line with experimental results, and that there is a non-zero $v_3$ value for Cu+Cu collisions at a 7.7 GeV/nucleon incident velocity.

This research introduces the concept of SimSura, a novel robotic system capable of generating three-dimensional structures on demand. By utilizing a single 6-DoF robotic arm, paired with an end-effector consisting of an electric motor, a camera, and an infrared sensor, SimSura can simultaneously plan, monitor, and execute the creation of structures. A key innovation of SimSura is the integration of an active gripper, which allows for adaptive construction of beams while accounting for uncertainty in their positioning. Moreover, SimSura's architecture is designed to facilitate creation of beams in any 3D space, and its image processing capabilities allow for real-time uncertainty assessment and feedback. Ultimately, SimSura's capabilities are showcased through experimental results demonstrating its potential for accurate simultaneous structure creation and uncertainty reduction.

A key challenge in deep learning for autonomous driving is to improve model performance.
A potential solution involves pre-training neural networks on large datasets.
A critical consideration involves selecting tasks that yield optimal pre-training results.
This work examines the efficacy of pre-training a monocular depth assessment task.
Initially, we evaluate depth assessment loss functions to determine which performs best.
Next, we compare these losses across different network architectures to assess their robustness.
Ultimately, we assess whether these depths enable better initialisation of a semantic segmentation network than randomly initialised counterparts.
Our research reveals that state-of-the-art depth assessment loss functions outperform their equivalents in classification loss functions and provide well-defined network weights that facilitate deeper initialisation.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau, often utilized in analyzing ordinal data, suffers from inefficiency when estimated through traditional methods due to its computationally intensive nature. This issue is particularly pronounced in datasets comprising multiple time points. This paper introduces the development of efficient estimation and hypothesis testing methods for Kendall's tau by utilizing weighted U-statistics, and presents large sample theory as a foundation for these results. Furthermore, a practical implementation involving data weighting and sample splitting is presented to simplify the implementation process. These techniques are supported by simulation studies and real-world applications demonstrating their efficacy.

The integration of Edge Intelligence (EI) in vehicle networks provides a platform for vehicles to use their data for community benefit, with the edge cloud facilitating this by processing information from multiple source vehicles. However, the risk of exposing personal vehicle data to cyber threats necessitates the use of Differential Privacy (DP) techniques to ensure data protection. This paper aims to establish a unified framework for DP in EI-empowered vehicle networks, taking into account the unique challenges posed by vehicle mobility, resource limitations, and data diversity. We introduce two DP protection strategies - local and centralized, each with their own computational and communication trade-offs. Furthermore, we address vehicle data heterogeneity and develop an EI model combining local weighted voting and edge federated learning to optimize local and edge model training. We analyze the DP protection effectiveness of our proposed framework through numerical evaluations using real vehicle trajectories, demonstrating the balance between model accuracy and data privacy through quantitative evaluation.
This paper introduces a novel method for generating Euler Topology surfaces and examines its application in the context of the Kondo model.

This study focuses on the intricate dynamics of the Holling-Tanner predator-prey model with strong Allee effect in prey population dynamics. We establish the conditions for prey extinction and coexistence, as well as the stability of the prey-Allee equilibrium and the Allee-free coexistence equilibrium, as these outcomes are inherently stable. We also demonstrate the existence of limit cycles arising from Hopf bifurcations, as well as double Hopf and Bogdanov-Takens points, using direct observation and the Routh-Hurwitz criterion, as well as numerical simulations.

Our previous research on the comprehensive pivot method for solving linear programming tasks has led to the conclusion that an additional, practically attainable constraint is necessary for the feasibility of each intermediate iteration. In this study, we present a modified iteration approach that eliminates the requirement for this constraint by incorporating a step that guarantees a uniform decrease in the Euclidean norm of the gradient vector along the direction of the active variable vector. This results in the establishment of the ultimate iteration limit and provides a theoretical foundation for the effectiveness of the comprehensive pivot method.

We have established that the NK1 of a modular group N(R) from Leslie Baker's construction (G. Leih, 1995) is built from a module's basis for a free module U over a ring R and an infinite set of units from its associated graded components, all together with an invertible matrix.

The extraction of a mass from the most prevalent top quark production event, top quark associated with a jet, poses significant challenges due to the substantial influence of gauge dependencies and higher-order corrections. These complexities are particularly pronounced when attempting to derive a mass from the observed invariant mass of the quark system, despite the established relationship between off-shell and higher-order corrections. In this study, a novel approach is introduced to quantify gauge dependencies, enabling the separation of off-shell and jet mass contributions, and thereby facilitating a more accurate extraction of a mass from these events.

This study investigates the potential of Vision Transformers (ViTs), a state-of-the-art computer vision technology, for deepfake detection. Initially, we evaluate the image classification performance of ViTs with varying image size inputs to determine the optimal image size for accuracy and efficiency. Following this analysis, we examine the adaptability of ViTs to transfer learning scenarios and evaluate their effectiveness in two prominent deepfake datasets. Our results indicate that ViTs achieve notable results on both datasets, albeit requiring a larger number of parameters compared to traditional ViTs architectures. Notably, ViTs exhibit exceptional robustness against data augmentation techniques and various attack methods. Our comprehensive analysis and findings for the first time reveal the effectiveness of ViTs as a domain-adaptation tool for challenging deepfake detection tasks, particularly in large-scale image datasets.

This research explores the application of Deep Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Vehicles. Based on the Principle of Reinforcement Learning, we aim to develop an optimal control policy for a fully autonomous vehicle. To this end, we propose a Deep Q-Network model that can learn and refine its strategy through trial and error, leveraging the Demonstration-Matching Reinforcement Learning framework's benefits. By integrating demonstrated behavior into the training process, our model converges more rapidly and effectively than traditional methods. The results of our proposed model's performance are illustrated through video demonstrations.

To address the evaluation time bias in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms, which can lead to suboptimal solutions and inaccurate fitness assessments, we introduce a novel frequency-based parent selection technique in this research. By mitigating evaluation time bias, we enhance algorithm performance. To this end, we developed a specific index that accounts for a parent's evaluation time when choosing frequencies for selection, and implemented our approach in a parallel NSGA-III algorithm for testing. Comparative studies revealed that our proposed approach successfully counteracts evaluation time bias and yields superior algorithm performance compared to a standard selection method.

The identification of exoplanets primarily relies on two methods: microlensing and the direct detection of a companion's gravitational effect on a host star's motion. A recently discovered exoplanet, identified through microlensing, has been re-analyzed using data from Keck's Near-Infrared Camera and Spectrograph, resulting in the detection of a companion's perturbation indicative of a gravitationally bound system. This exoplanet system, identified as OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, consists of a 3.6 Jupiter mass planet orbiting its host star at a distance of 2.3 astronomical units. A second analysis, utilizing the astrometric method, confirms the system's existence, estimating the mass of the planet as 7.2 to 8.2 Earth masses. A more precise calculation, combining both methods, yields a mass estimate of 7.0 to 8.2 Earth masses, with an orbital distance of approximately 2.32 astronomical units. This exoplanet is notable for being the coldest known Earth-sized planet, with an estimated temperature of around 50 Kelvin.

A general method to approach the non-commutative Lindbladian generator was developed. This method involved expanding the Lindbladian into a series of terms based on the magnitude of an auxiliary parameter $\lambda$, whose small magnitude reflects the magnitude of the oscillation frequency $\omega$. This frequency can be significant, but should be less than the inverse of the parameter $\lambda$. This expansion was shown to be useful for a broad range of physical systems, including a two-level atom interacting with an oscillating coherent state field, a coherent state's effect on a two-level atom when the oscillation frequency is much higher than the coherent driving amplitude, and a two-level atom interacting with a coherent state field under high-rate detuning conditions. These scenarios demonstrated the ability of this method to find the quasi-energy spectrum and quasi-Stark states of the system without resorting to a full Floquet Hamiltonian treatment. This method was also found to be able to reproduce known results in the low-order terms of the expansion, such as the quasi-energy and Stark states of a two-level atom driven by a laser field, and to yield new insights, such as a periodic modulation of the quasi-energy and quasi-Stark states of a two-level atom in certain time scales when the oscillation frequency is much higher than both the coherent driving amplitude and detuning.

Neutron depolarization is utilized to quantify the irregular fluctuations in magnetic fields.  Studies on various materials, including metals and magnetic flux cores, have been conducted to assess the source of fluctuations.  This study, focusing on cerium-rhodium alloys (CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$), used incoherent neutron scattering for a comprehensive analysis.  By varying rhodium concentration, researchers were able to examine how depolarization correlates with solid solutions and how it diverges near critical points.  The results indicate high levels of alloy magnetic field fluctuations in close proximity to solid solutions, suggesting that these fluctuations are a critical precursor to neutron solidification.  This suggests that fluctuations, rather than an ordered magnetic structure, are responsible for solidification in these neutron-scattering alloys.

A comprehensive investigation of high-mass star-formation region G176.51+00.20 was conducted, focusing on the origins and characteristics of its 21-cm line features. These features, which exhibit self-absorbed patterns, were found to be linked with large-scale filaments. A detailed analysis of these features revealed that their temperatures and velocities align with those of the surrounding interstellar medium. It was observed that the formation of these features can be attributed to a combination of factors, including thermal effects and complex velocity patterns within the region. Additionally, it was discovered that a significant fraction of these features, which have masses of less than 1-10 solar masses, play a crucial role in understanding star formation processes, particularly in regions with low metallicity.

We present a type of beta number whose greedy expansion exhibits a gap between 0 and 1, and a beta number with the shortest possible interval for this gap. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain avaricious beta numbers also possess a gap in their greedy expansions, and calculate a lower limit on the size of this gap. These findings are founded on the use of Z-transforms to examine properties of beta numbers' greedy expansions.

Dedicated to studying charge conjugation parity violations in Dzero, the LHCb experiment uses the LHC's data collected in 2011, involving hadronic Bs decays to detect a specific angle representation. To this end, the decay products are analyzed with approximately 1.2 inverse femtobarns worth of data, pinpointing the phase difference between vector and scalar mesons as -22 degrees plus or minus 21, with an estimated 19 degrees systematic error margin, thus providing a precise measure of charge conjugation parity violations in relevant decays.

This study aims to resolve the issue of adapting pre-trained deep neural networks to handle images with distinct statistical properties. This problem is particularly challenging in dynamic environments where training data may differ significantly from real-world inputs due to the evolution of data distributions over time. A new framework is proposed to compare various domain transfer techniques for deep neural networks, which are evaluated using classification accuracy and model weight stability. Experimental results demonstrate that our evaluation framework is effective and yield interesting findings, which suggest that evaluating domain adaptation techniques in online settings may be more appropriate.

This paper explores a unique demonstration of geometric proof by visually showcasing the impossibility of fitting an additional triangle of the same size into a set of three non-overlapping triangles within a triangular frame, all while visually conveying that no matter the size or arrangement of the three initial triangles, they can never fit with a fourth one. This concept is demonstrated through the use of dynamic geometry software.

This study introduces the Parameterized Graph Interpreter (PGI), a novel search-based approach to design graph neural networks (GNNs) that incorporates pre-existing gnn modules as its base units. By utilizing PGI, we can effectively identify the most suitable search architecture and parameterize it with fixed values, thus avoiding the need for a labor-intensive end-to-end search without prior weight initializations. Our research shows that PGIs produce competitive results and outperforms pre-trained weight initializations in both a straightforward and complex task, while also demonstrating its ability to find a search architecture that matches the performance of the top-ranking Evolving Graph Neural Networks (E-GNN) algorithm, a state-of-the-art search method, but at a significantly reduced computational cost and time.

We analyzed the substructure within the RXCJ032.2-4420 galaxy cluster using multiple methods including X-ray data, Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, and optical data. By combining X-ray and Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect measurements, we identified the cluster's total mass as 1.73 x 10^14 solar masses. By applying various techniques to X-ray data, we discovered a substructure in the southern region with an estimated size of 1.1 x 10^14 solar masses. Additionally, we detected a second substructure in the western part with a size of 1.8 x 10^13 solar masses. By utilizing the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, we confirmed the existence of the western substructure. We also identified a third substructure in the eastern part with an estimated size of 2.8 x 10^13 solar masses. By cross-correlating X-ray data with optical galaxy data, we discovered the presence of this substructure in the eastern part. We found that the cluster's substructures are not in hydrostatic equilibrium. We discovered that the cluster is undergoing a merger event. By analyzing the cluster's substructure, we found that it is likely that the cluster is in the process of merging.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Module (LMM), a novel type of recurrent neural network, has emerged as a leading contender in processing time-series data, including forecasting and outlier detection tasks. Its simplified design and high performance make it particularly appealing for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Nonetheless, the most efficient existing methods for training LMM still face a significant bottleneck, the CPU-based solver for the Schwinger-Keldysh (SK) integral, which is essential for calculating the output. To overcome this limitation, we successfully parallelized the CPU solver, thereby reducing training times by up to 80 times. Our approach leverages the LMM's inherent spatial and temporal parallelism to enable fast training. Additionally, we conducted a thorough investigation into the memory module's design space and the impact of memory operations on training, shedding light on the complexities of optimizing LMM.

This review outlines the current knowledge of experimentally detected neutral particles, with a primary focus on previously invisible particles that have been identified through direct and high-energy beam experiments. The discussion then shifts to speculative theories of new neutral particles. The naturally occurring particles, with their known masses and interaction strengths, are examined as a baseline for understanding hidden sectors. The standard model of weakly-interacting particles is then described as a bridge to hidden sectors of theories beyond the standard model. The direct search for invisible particles has a long history, beginning with Eötvös's search for dark matter. The discussion on beam experiments starts by examining the null results of searches for low-energy forces between macroscopic objects. The review then delves into high-energy beam experiments, highlighting searches for inelastic particle collisions that involve newly discovered particles. The discussion on production mechanisms highlights the role of gauge boson mixing in particle creation. The review concludes by examining the constraints on particle couplings, emphasizing the importance of both weak and gravitational interactions in particle search experiments.

A language game model is introduced where individuals develop personal communication systems by assigning labels to traits they exhibit, thus allowing for the analysis of how these systems interact with evolving characteristics. These systems also enable exchange of genetic and cultural information. Due to variations in perceived utility, agents migrate to neighboring communities in search of a better quality of life. Initially used to model sexual selection and cultural transmission, this framework has been effective in producing a diverse array of labeled characteristics, resembling real-world observations. However, a challenge arises where two communities might utilize the same label to describe distinct traits, leading to confusion and communication breakdown. This issue stems from a lack of linguistic consistency among the labeling systems. To address this problem, a new game with migrating agents is studied, allowing for the investigation of labeling strategies that a wise agent would adopt in order to maximize the likelihood of being correctly understood by others, thus ensuring effective communication across different populations.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly used to solve partial differential equations. Their performance largely depends on choosing appropriate optimization parameters. This study examines how incorporating momentum into PINNs affects their optimization. By combining the insights from neural tangent kernel theory and PINN research, we find that adding momentum reduces the bias toward learning simple functions early on, thereby allowing for a more balanced initial focus on complex functions. This discovery holds true for a range of problems under a few practical assumptions. By building upon existing research that has shown the benefits of momentum, our results provide further evidence that utilizing momentum within PINNs can be advantageous. A thorough discussion of how early optimization behavior impacts PINN's overall accuracy is also included in our findings.

We study a two-dimensional system representing coupled differential equations, which models the interaction of two large-scale elastic waves undergoing damping, first introduced by Kelvin and Voigt, and we examine how this system responds to external disturbances, particularly those that are localized, which are responsible for carrying energy along with the waves. We prove the existence and long-term stability of weak, large-distance waves of any given speed, which are analogous to the waves of Kelvin and Voigt, and we show that these waves' derivatives decay over time, achieving optimal, exponential rates. Moreover, we examine how the system's long-term behavior is influenced when it's disturbed in a confined area, and we show that under the right conditions of smoothness and decay, the long-term behavior of disturbed waves is similar to that of the coupled waves, which are analogous to the waves of Kelvin and Voigt, and we show that when it's disturbed, the system quickly stabilizes around a wave of any given speed, which is analogous to the waves of Kelvin and Voigt, and we show that under the right conditions of smoothness, the long-term behavior of disturbed waves is similar to that of the coupled waves, which are analogous to the waves of Kelvin and Voigt, and we show that a small amount of memory in the damping mechanism can lead to a significant difference in the long-term behavior of disturbed waves, which is analogous to the coupled waves of Kelvin and Voigt, and we show that under the right conditions of smoothness,

Deep Reinforcement Learning has proven highly effective in numerous applications, yet it has significant drawbacks including the requirement for extensive rewards and a lack of interpretability. In complex environments with incomplete reward structures, reward engineering becomes time-consuming and challenging. On another front, black-box models struggle to provide clear insights into their reasoning processes for high-stakes decisions. In response, we propose a model-based hierarchical learning approach and an explanation generation method based on inductive logic programming, which enable agents to derive rewards and policies from loosely defined goals and natural language explanations for selected actions.

A long-standing concept in quantum mechanics suggests that any process can be reversed given perfect knowledge, with traditional irreversible processes requiring degradation in quality. However, recent research suggests this idea may be expanded to include information as a resource. To test this theory, we investigated the thermodynamics of a two-level atom in a coherent light field and discovered that a sudden change in the atom's coupling to the environment can prevent equilibrium from being reached even in ideal conditions. This phenomenon is not explained by standard irreversible theory and highlights the complex nature of non-reversible quantum processes.

We've developed a novel, stochastic variant of the Fenton-Schoen type challenge. It involves determining the optimal worst-case effect of a linear combination of functions on a random variable. By framing the problem in this context, we can leverage existing research from the Fenton-Steineisen approach to yield a novel proof of the Schumacher Theorem and potentially yield a more precise version of Schumacher's result. Furthermore, the framework can be applied to investigate various statistical challenges such as robust estimation of a random variable's expectation and the robust estimation of a random variable's support.

The study of particle dark matter interactions with $^6$Li within the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment has been conducted using an analytical model. This investigation has shown that the experiment's sensitivity can effectively rule out certain particles between 0.1 and 10 MeV, making it possible to exclude numerous existing dark matter candidates. To compare with other technologies, the study has considered detection rates in experiments employing $^3$He spin-dependent interactions as well as those employing electron recoil, revealing that the LUX-ZEPLIN's sensitivity can competitively surpass that of other technologies in specific scenarios, particularly in comparison to experiments employing electron recoil.

Blind Image Restoration (BIR) focuses on restoring a degraded image based solely on its single observation when the imaging process's parameters are unknown. A previous approach, Key Image Restoration, assumed pixel values followed a log-normal distribution and identified the best mapping from a key image to the original by optimizing loss function performance, even without knowing the imaging parameters. However, assuming pixel values are log-normally distributed is not always accurate, and even if they were, finding the optimal key image becomes computationally impractical due to the enormous search space. Our proposed approach, Blind Image Restoration based on Kernel Mixture (BIRMK), improves upon this limitation by using a kernel function, specifically employing a Gaussian mixture as a kernel function, to model the image's pixel value distribution. By representing pixel value density as a kernel function, our approach allows for efficient computation of key images, which in turn enables effective degradation reversal even when the imaging parameters are unknown.

A recent concept, termed nonassociative Yang-Baxter equation, was introduced in 2019 as a dual framework for representation theory of bialgebras. This paper introduces a nonuniform equation equivalent to the relative R-matrix equation in this representation theory context. It was demonstrated that the nonuniform equation has practical applications in representation theory, particularly in constructing solutions to the relative R-matrix equation via direct sum and meromorphic gluing techniques. Moreover, a class of solutions to nonuniform equation was identified as cone cones, which possess a distinct geometric property under the dual action of a corolla. This section of the article showcases a method for constructing cones, initially developed in 2013 as a representation theory tool.

Formal verification has long been a widely used approach for determining the correctness of software. The challenge lies in communicating program expectations to a broad audience, particularly given that traditional specification languages are difficult for non-experts to grasp. To address this issue, a language called Natural Hoare was developed, using logical formulas in plain English to describe program correctness. To ensure these specifications are rigorously verified, a formal system was created that translates Natural Hoare specifications into a usable format and validates them against actual code. This formal system, known as Natural Hoare Logic, provides a direct way to validate Natural Hoare specifications, underpinning each rule with a simple English explanation. Through careful design, Natural Hoare Logics were successfully implemented in a proof assistant, and its effectiveness was demonstrated with several correctness verification examples.

Consensus algorithms are crucial for coordinating distributed systems, but they are highly sensitive to node failures, particularly in cases where nodes provide incorrect information. The RCanonical algorithm is a robust variant of Canopus, designed to withstand both node failures and the occurrence of Byzantine errors. By incorporating Byzantine-resilient data aggregation, RCanus maintains Canopus's performance characteristics while improving its overall robustness. Theoretical evaluations and real-world experiments demonstrate that RCanus outperforms Canopus in terms of robustness and exhibits comparable latency and throughput, even when no faulty nodes are present. Furthermore, simulations and experiments reveal that RCanus has a negligible overhead in processing additional checks when dealing with up to one faulty node, maintaining Canopus's efficiency.

To determine the bending modulus of lipid membranes containing cholesterol, 
we used an advanced molecular dynamics technique based on the undulating
membrane approach, which yielded results comparable to those obtained through
the traditional undulating plane method. We found that by using an 
optimized wave function based on a combination of two modes, we achieved a more
efficient and accurate estimation. We observed variations in the bending modulus
of the lipid assembly depending on cholesterol concentration. We found that the
clustering tendency of cholesterol increased the rigidity of the membrane in the
case of DOPC but had a negligible effect in the case of DPPC. We found that the
clustering threshold for cholesterol was around 20-25 mol%.

By applying the Poisson-Lie deformation to the Einstein-Hilbert action, we derive a loop quantum astrophysical model based on the Bardeen-McFadden metric, providing a quantum correction for spherically symmetric spacetimes. This model serves as an alternative to black holes and neutron stars, and we investigate its properties and those of its event horizon. Furthermore, we consider the thermal characteristics and entropy of the system in the context of this quantum corrected spacetime.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog presents its preliminary findings, documenting 100 high-energy cosmic ray air showers recorded during the initial phase of its operation. With an energy resolution of 15%, this catalog identifies the highest energy events exceeding 50 EeV, with energies formally estimated at $\mathrm{10^{\,log_{10}\, (1000\, EeV)^2-\,0.15^2\,EeV^2\,log_{10}\,S_{\mathrm{p.m.}}\,}}$. Spanning 23 months of data collection between June 2000 and February 2003, this phase utilized an initial 25% of the full detector configuration. This publication serves as the foundational document for those seeking recorded air showers with an energy threshold of at least 50 EeV.

In practical applications of object detection, understanding the uncertainty of predictions is crucial. This study introduces BayesOD, a Bayesian approach to evaluate the uncertainty of deep object detection models. It modifies object localization and classification tasks to align with Bayesian model averaging, incorporating probabilistic neural network outputs through a Monte Carlo sampling technique. Furthermore, this study develops an unsupervised reliability diagram refinement method, enhancing the accuracy of uncertainty assessments. Experiments were conducted on MS-COCO, demonstrating that BayesOD effectively correlates predicted uncertainty with actual error, outperforming alternative methods in both coverage and calibration aspects.

This paper presents an innovative approach to predicting traffic patterns based on a novel concept - traffic moving segments (TMS). TMS captures the inherent non-stationarity of traffic time series data. To the best of our knowledge, our proposed method is a first in using TMS for traffic prediction. We introduce a novel technique that involves a support vector regression model to forecast the traffic value corresponding to each individual TMS. To determine which TMS to utilize for prediction at a given time step, we introduce a novel technique involving a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network that forecasts the moving segment itself, which then determines the prediction model. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method against existing state-of-the-art traffic forecasting techniques using real-world datasets and our results demonstrate that our proposed method consistently achieves superior performance across all tested scenarios.

We broaden the concept of rewriting in finite sets within the framework of Gray classes. This extension is demonstrated to be applicable to arbitrary objects in the Gray category, encompassing directed graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a length-based confluence criterion, which is shown to be beneficial in the context of consistency applications. Specifically, we establish a link between any directed graph and a set of permutations, and prove that a terminating directed graph rewriting system, featuring a left identity and left cancellative property, is also left-confluent.

The hippocampus, a critical memory center in the brain, is now understood to be composed of distinct sub-regions, which may operate differently.  Hippocampal sclerosis, a more complex condition than previously assumed, involves the degradation of certain hippocampal areas, leading to impaired memory.  Despite the ongoing research on the region, medical imaging still often treats the hippocampus as a single entity, which could hinder accurate diagnosis and treatment.  To bridge this knowledge gap, a study has been conducted to evaluate the potential of artificial intelligence to automatically segment the hippocampus into its distinct sub-regions, using algorithms that could assist in identifying hippocampal sclerosis.  By applying a specific deep learning model to a dataset of 104 hippocampi, the study achieved a segmentation accuracy of 87.2% and 84.1% for intra-class and inter-class metrics, respectively, and found that adding more training data could improve its performance.  Furthermore, the study has also explored the potential of using partial hippocampal volume measurements to predict cognitive decline in patients with mild cognitive impairment, which could help in developing personalized treatment plans.

In evaluating the computational complexity of the pigeonhole problem, we focus on the mode of action employed by quantum circuits. Our research reveals that circuits featuring a moderate number of transversal qumodes exhibit polynomial-time computational capabilities, specifically the ability to calculate minimal subsets within the super-PSP problem containing no duplicates. This contrasts with circuits utilizing an exponentially large number of qumodes used transversally, akin to quantum pseudorandom number generators (QPRNG), capable of solving super-PSP but failing to determine minimal no-duplicates subsets. Furthermore, we investigate the transversal mode of action in relation to Pigeonholе, discovering that it necessitates either a low or extremely high number of qumodes used transversally for effective resolution. Notably, an intermediate quantity of transversal qumodes hinders the solution of Pigeonhole through quantum combinatorics.

In recent years, investigations into the impact of the Cosmic Ray Anisotropy on satellites and electronic components in Earth's low orbit have gained significant attention. This research paper investigates the anisotropic capture of Cosmic Rays at low Earth orbit by utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation and comparing the simulations to measured Cosmic Ray data, taking into account the influence of Anisotropy on particles captured from outside the Earth's magnetosphere.

Deep Graph Neural Networks have become a vital tool in machine learning, network science, and related fields. Nonetheless, GNNs face significant challenges, such as oversimplified model architectures, limited expressiveness, and poor generalization capabilities in real-world scenarios. To address these issues, a novel Deep GNN framework is proposed, centered around two key components: a Pyramidal Shrinkage Module and the Local Topology Link Reconfiguration. By optimizing local graph topology and designing the Pyramidal Shrinkage framework, it is possible to enhance local feature representation and global message aggregation efficiency. This, in turn, enables more effective GNN design and improved performance in real-world applications. PyG, PyTorch-Geometric, is employed to validate the proposed framework's performance.

This study presents a novel application of the Huber approach within differential privacy, utilizing it to resolve low-rank matrix fulfillment problems. Building upon differentially private matrix factorization, the current work addresses multiple matrix completion tasks. First, we provide an in-depth examination of the Laplace mechanism and its role in private low-rank matrix completion. Subsequently, the current work introduces and validates the Huber approach for low-rank matrix fulfillment problems involving non-smooth loss functions, such as those found in robust matrix completion and orthogonal tensor completion. Empirical results for robust orthogonal tensor completion demonstrate the efficacy of the Huber mechanism in enhancing privacy outcomes.

We introduce a physical model for the scattering and absorption properties of interstellar dust, incorporating a combination of grains with two distinct compositions, each having distinct sizes, and a combination of thermal emission components resulting from these four thermal emission components. This cohesively represents interstellar extinction, emission, and polarization. The PAH component accounts for ultraviolet and optical (UV-O) optical polarization, while a combination of silicate and carbon-based grains make up the near-infrared (NIR) and infrared (IR) emission. The PAH and a combination of smaller silicate grains contribute to the near-IR (NIR) and IR emission, respectively. The model successfully captures the observed trends in extinction, emission, and polarization, and accurately represents data from a combination of space-based telescopes, including the Spitzer, Herschel, and the WISE.

A low-mass star called CIDA 1, which has a mass similar to Jupiter's, has a surrounding protoplanetary disk.
