A significant number of massive early-type galaxies are known to exhibit visible tidal tails, indicating that they are either in the process of or have recently undergone a merger. This study examines the relationship between tidal features and the merger rates of early-type galaxies across three distinct redshift ranges at high resolution. Data from 110,000 galaxies within the 0.1 to 0.9 redshift interval, categorized into 10,000 early-type galaxies and 110,000 lenticular and elliptical galaxies, are analyzed. This investigation compares the characteristics of galaxies with and without tidal features in terms of surface brightness, surface area, and the luminosity ratio between a galaxy and its tidal counterpart. This analysis reveals that galaxies with tidal features are, on average, 0.5 magnitudes fainter than their counterparts, with a surface brightness that is 2.5 to 3.5 magnitudes per square arcsecond brighter. Notably, galaxies with tidal features are observed to be in the process of merging more frequently than those without, with a merger rate that is 1.5 to 2 times higher. This study estimates the fraction of galaxies with tidal features across various redshifts, revealing a trend where the fraction of galaxies with tidal features decreases with increasing redshift, peaking at around 10 percent at redshifts below 0.5. This study further refines our understanding of the tidal features in massive

A new gravitomagnetic effect is suggested to be responsible for the rapid movement of T Tauri stars, and it may also explain the formation of large cosmic structures such as galaxies and clusters. In particular, variations in a T Tauri star's spin axis orientation could lead to changes in the direction of gravitomagnetic fields, which in turn could exert repulsive forces on nearby matter. As a result, a gravitomagnetic effect rather than attraction, could be responsible for the formation of these cosmic structures. A new theory is proposed to investigate the possibility of repulsive gravitomagnetic forces at various scales, and it is found that these forces can be comparable to the primary gravitational force. In particular, a time-dependent gravitomagnetic field, characterized by an angle $\theta_G$, may lead to the emission of gravitons, and it is proposed that this phenomenon, rather than jets, may be responsible for the emission of high-energy radiation observed from T Tauri stars.

Recent research has shown that radio emissions from Fast Radio Bursts may originate and propagate separately.  Observations of the Vela pulsar demonstrate that radio and microwave (H-band) emissions can be emitted as distinct pulses, while a study of twelve (8-16 GHz) FRBs revealed the potential for radio and microwave (H-band) emissions to be delayed up to 0.1 seconds.  This delay would support models in which relativistic particles are injected into surrounding plasma at separate times.  We propose a method to constrain both simultaneous and time-lagged multi-frequency optical emission.  By combining the known upper limits on simultaneous radio and microwave (H-band) optical emission, our findings indicate that any H-band optical emission is highly constrained.  Conversely, H-band optical emission with up to 0.1 s delays is limited by an order of magnitude.  These constraints on time-lagged optical emission are applicable to various emission models, such as synchrotron self-absorption, inverse Compton scattering, and radio recombination lines.  Fast Radio Burst optical emission is thus expected to be either highly constrained or delayed, in contrast to expectations from simultaneous radio and (optical) microwave (H-band) emission models.

High-power laser systems have become essential tools in various fields, encompassing industrial manufacturing, cutting-edge research, defense applications, and medical treatments. Laser design is a highly intricate process that combines theoretical knowledge with practical experience to achieve optimal results. This challenge is compounded by the diverse requirements of laser systems, unique to their respective fields of application. Nevertheless, advancements in computational methods and machine learning techniques have made it possible to model laser systems and analyze their performance using algorithms and reverse engineering techniques. This paper showcases several high-power laser systems and their applications, as well as the role of machine learning in laser design and analysis, reverse engineering, and simulations. Reverse engineering techniques used in high-power laser systems are also discussed.

The success of state-of-the-art language models in generating human-quality text has led researchers to explore incorporating visual controls like summaries, edits, and explanations to manage these models. This integration empowers creators to produce text with control, flexibility, and efficiency by leveraging visual tools. This paper investigates how incorporating visual controls like pausing, editing, and restarting within text generation enables creators to exercise more control over the language modeling process. By incorporating visual controls, researchers discovered that text generation could be retrained and repositioned in the fluency-accuracy space, ultimately allowing for the creation of more accurate texts. By integrating visual controls, researchers observed improvements in the flexibility of text creation, including the ability to explore multiple options, express uncertainty, and adjust generation parameters. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating visual controls as a more effective approach compared to traditional fine-tuning methods, paving the way for the development of language models that are collaborative and interactive.

We present an innovative modification to the RingCT technique, enabling users to securely and quickly share transaction data with a trusted party, thereby allowing them to complete RingCT transactions in a manner reminiscent of instant payment systems. Our enhanced RingCT is now nucleus-compatible.

A beam scan is a comprehensive beam characterization technique that measures the brightness distribution of complex beam arrays, such as those comprising multiple sub-beams or featuring deliberate and random variations in phase, amplitude, and polarization. This beam scan approach, versatile in analyzing both narrow and wide, coherent and incoherent arrays, provides valuable insights for determining the true beam coverage and performance of beamforming antennas, and can also be utilized to analyze biological tissue and other targets with difficult reflectance properties.

A promising approach to complex data-driven problems is to combine advanced scientific knowledge with large datasets. However, collaborative projects often face challenges due to data holders' privacy concerns. This issue is particularly pressing for scientists on a global stage. This work proposes a novel data exchangable protocol to facilitate secure and private data collaborations. The protocol leverages cutting-edge homomorphic encryption technology to allow encrypted data analysis without compromising information confidentiality. This research explores practical implementations of data collaboration among cloud services, including our open-source software built on top of Google's Tensorflow framework to support deep learning model training. The experiment results demonstrate the protocol's effectiveness in enabling secure data collaborations. The related source code is available on GitHub for cloudflenc modelfor more detailed reference.

This study proposes that the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ $(n=1,2)$ is triggered by a hadronic loop process. In this mechanism, an intermediate resonance, denoted as $f_0(500)$, is involved, and its behavior is described using the Bethe-Salpeter formalism. Calculations based on the dispersion relation and one-loop counter term are used to fit the invariant mass distribution observed in the LHCb experiment, revealing that the coupling constant between the $f_0(500)$ and the pion pair is significantly stronger than that between the latter.

This study proposes a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD that combines quantized weight constraints with interval-based optimization to train quantized neural networks more efficiently than traditional quantization methods. AskewSGD is an iterative algorithm that uses a tailored variant of stochastic gradient descent to explore the parameter space and converge towards an optimal solution. By allowing weights to transition between their quantized and continuous states, AskewSGD enables the training of quantized neural networks using standard deep learning frameworks. Additionally, AskewSGD can be integrated into existing neural network architecture design processes, facilitating the development of quantized models with enhanced accuracy and reduced computational requirements.

This article discusses recent advancements in the field of soft robot control, specifically focusing on model driven approaches. Research in this area is divided into three main categories: theoretical, applied, and open challenges. Challenges in this domain include developing accurate physical models for soft robots, which is a crucial step in achieving optimal performance. By identifying areas of improvement, this study provides a roadmap for future research in soft robot technology.

A specific subgroup of the Jacobi group has been identified as a key relation between the Siegel-Jacobi module's polarized complex structure and the classical Jacobi form's complex structure. All previous studies of this subgroup relied on an incorrect representation, whereas our research identifies and corrects this error and provides the correct one, a crucial component of the semi-classical limit of the Heisenberg-Jacobi co-representation of the metaplectic-Jacobi group.

Recent advances in table recognition tasks have been made by applying language modeling techniques, which treat task-specific inputs as special tokens. Building on this trend, we explore how natural language inference can be applied to table-related fact verification through textual and structural analyses. However, we find that direct adaptation of language modeling techniques to fact verification results in suboptimal accuracy, likely due to complex interdependencies among facts in terms of correctness and semantic meaning. To address this challenge, we investigate the effectiveness of decomposition methods, specifically hierarchical and iterative approaches, in enhancing model performance. Our findings reveal that hierarchical decomposition yields significant performance gains, particularly in queries requiring multi-hop reasoning. Moreover, our study indicates that employing language modeling techniques after decomposing queries can yield better results, thereby establishing a new baseline for fact verification tasks.

Our method introduces an unsupervised approach to condition deep learning models like GANs in areas such as image and music synthesis. This technique maximizes the information content within a low-dimensional representation, resulting in a compact, well-organized condition space. This is achieved through consistent training based on a shared generator for both samples and condition sequences, combined with a novel loss function utilizing information theory. The condition space learning is further enhanced by a variable encoding loss, promoting a well-structured, information-rich mapping. This strategy leads to improved outcomes with models that to date have multiple parameters, demonstrated in experiments with CF-GAN and CNFGAN. Additionally, our research reveals that incorporating a condition space significantly increases the realness of models' output, even in cases where the space is small.

MCMC algorithms can be developed using various techniques to insert proposals that enhance efficiency over random suggestions. This article introduces a general framework for comparing Markov chain samplers linked by a common proposal scheme. Utilizing the concept of coupling from the past, the study evaluates nonasymptotic exponential convergence rates of coupled Markov chains. By comparing the expected coupling times, distinct step metrics for linked and unlinked samplers are introduced, offering insights into step efficiency. As an application, the article investigates coupled sampling algorithms based on trees, demonstrating the contrast of several related sampling techniques including Glazek and Kerstan, Kingman, and Rebolledo and Wang.

For any given graph, we need to calculate the shortest path distances between all nodes, but when the graph is vast and complex, we seek a more compact distance labeling system that enables us to determine the distances between any two nodes without relying on the entire graph structure, thus enhancing our ability to calculate distances even after the removal of a single node or its associated edge. We have developed a new compact distance labeling system for planar graphs, allowing us to compute distances with an accuracy within a factor of ten, using only $O(m)$ space, where $m$ denotes the maximum possible shortest path distance, compactness of $O(n)$, and resilience to a single node or edge failure for any $n$-node planar graph.

In this study, we investigate the correlations of the Bose-Hubbard model with tunable driving and dissipation as a function of both time and frequency, with an initial condition of a Mott insulator state. By numerically evaluating the two-particle correlation functions using a world-line tensor network approach, we explore both temporal and spectral domains. In the absence of particle-hole interactions, we discover a decaying wave-like pattern in time and distinct peaks related to driving and dissipation frequencies in the spectrum. When considering particle-hole interactions, we find that they significantly alter correlation functions in both time and frequency, yielding a periodic oscillation in time and a periodic structure in the spectrum, with an initial decay. Our analysis reveals a connection between these interactions and outcomes seen in experiments involving cold Bose gases periodically driven with bichromatic laser light.

This research focuses on analyzing two types of elliptic equations in terms of their solvability and regularity: one in a form with divergence and another in a non-divergence shape. We investigate how the coefficients, particularly the drift term within a $L^2$ space, influence the regularity of the equation's solution and establish that an improved mathematical inequality, known as the John-Nashier-Pokhozayev inequality, can boost the measurable regularity of the solution up to a weak gradient level. Out-of-distribution detection is a critical component of deploying neural networks in real-world scenarios, yet current methods struggle with identifying certain types of anomalies. Although normal distribution layers have been utilized for OOD detection, their capacity is limited by assuming a normal distribution for all generated data points. In contrast, this research proposes a novel method that integrates sampling from the normal distribution with a normal mean, and also explores using the estimated network uncertainty for decision-making. Experimental outcomes demonstrate superior performance for this approach across various OOD datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques based on entropy and uncertainty estimates.

In this work, a Bose-condensed phase emerges due to intense heating caused by external driving forces, in contrast to the static conditions, where a similar system displays characteristics resembling a floquet-time-crystalline phase. The open nature of the system, where drift losses are significant, leads to a balance between heating and cooling rates, ultimately resulting in a phase transition characterized by the disappearance of Drude peaks as the heating rate increases. Our research highlights the possibility that optimal conditions for observing Bose condensation are found near the boundary of a parameter range where a topological phase transition occurs.

We provide a detailed proof of an enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle for the constrained right-hand side of solutions to the Monge-Are equation, offering a clear and unified approach that yields H\"older continuous functions with an optimal H\"older constant.

Recent developments in high-speed detection and electronics have enabled the creation of non-repetitive optical clocks with superior stability compared to existing optical and atomic clocks. Understanding the characteristics of noise in these new devices is crucial for maximizing their performance. In this study, we investigate the fluctuations in timing jitter affecting a non-repetitive optical clock based on single-shot time-stamping of a pulsed fiber laser, using statistical methods to describe its behavior. In addition to measuring the asymptotic stability of the system, we develop a model that captures the system's performance at various time scales by analyzing the distribution of pulse arrival times. In doing so, we not only identify the minimum achievable uncertainty in single-shot optical timing but also determine the minimum uncertainty possible with repeated measurements.

In Service Function Chaining (SFC), where network traffic is routed through specific services in a predetermined order, meeting real-time processing requirements is particularly challenging when facing multiple link failures. To address this issue, we propose a new approach, Fog-assisted Service Function Chain (FoSFC), which optimizes the management of resources in a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) environment supported by Fog computing. With the aid of Fault Tolerance Controllers located at Fog nodes, and considering real-time processing requirements and energy efficiency, our solution simultaneously restores failure, mitigates faults, and optimizes resource allocation. We evaluate the effectiveness of FoSFC using simulation experiments based on real-world network topologies, demonstrating its superiority in comparison to existing approaches.

This study investigates the impact of loss functions on neural network training through different gradients. We introduce a novel technique to dissect loss functions and analyze their influence on trained networks. By isolating the contributions of each loss function, we can understand their impact beyond average loss values. We evaluate this method on three computer vision tasks: image classification, object detection, and segmentation. Our experiments using the COCO dataset reveal that analyzing loss values alone is insufficient for selecting loss functions. We further show that analyzing gradients is not impacted by model architecture changes and loss functions can be combined in any order without significant loss accuracy variation.

We develop a new quantum lattice model, hyper-invariant MERA (HIMERA), which exhibits a power-law correlation function and possesses exact symmetry under a higher-dimensional group, $O(4,1)$. Similar to the tensor network MERA, HIMERA is composed of a series of tensors arranged in a hierarchy, yielding an efficient encoding scheme for bulk information with a error correction capability and short code distance. We establish that HIMERA can approximate a specific quantum encoding protocol used in the AdS/CFT framework, thereby implying its ability to replicate AdS-based error correction capabilities without sacrificing efficiency. We verify this by directly comparing the encoding paths derived from AdS holography and those generated from the geometry of the HIMERA model, revealing their similarity up to a substantial distance scale. We also demonstrate through direct calculation that the mutual information contained in the HIMERA model follows a power-rule pattern, thereby providing evidence for the model's ability to approximate AdS-based holographic error correction.

Previous studies have revealed that the Galactic Core area is densely populated by high luminosity stars connected in string-like patterns. Building upon earlier research, we examined the distances between these star filaments. We discovered that these separations tend to be wider for brighter filaments and that their distribution differs significantly from random arrangements of equally luminous objects.

The increasing adoption of renewable energy sources in distribution networks is creating challenges for network stability, particularly in maintaining prescribed voltage levels and reducing the need for energy storage systems. Research has shown that unnecessary high voltages can lead to increased network losses, prompting the development of novel control strategies to optimize preservation voltage and decrease the required energy storage capacity. This paper introduces a new approach to preservation voltage reduction by integrating primary and secondary networks in an interconnected framework. By modeling the relationships between these networks and considering the correlation of load demands, we propose a model-based predictive control strategy that leverages distributed control and estimated load profiles to minimize energy storage requirements while adhering to network operational constraints. By utilizing the network's operational constraints as control barriers, we ensure compliance with operational limits, even in the presence of modeling inaccuracies and modeling errors. Simulation results based on IEEE test systems demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy in reducing preservation voltage and decreasing the required energy storage capacity.

Multiarmed bandits have the potential to cause significant harm, which is why it's crucial to understand the conditions that influence decision-making in this context. Non-random processes, such as the nonrandom bandit problem, have emerged as a valuable area of study in decision-making theories to explore how individuals respond to events that are beyond their control. In this study, we investigate how people make choices when encountering non-random outcomes and introduce two notable phenomena: the delay pattern and the side-specific advantage. The delay pattern refers to the tendency for individuals to expect less harm in events associated with a higher probability of non-reward, whereas the side-specific advantage suggests that people make better choices in events associated with a lower probability of non-reward. To account for these phenomena, we propose a new theoretical model that incorporates arm-specific processing times and examine how these times impact decision-making under non-random conditions.

The success of AI systems largely relies on their ability to adapt to unpredictable environments, particularly human interaction, where subtle textual nuances significantly influence these adaptations.  Leveraging past experiences and utilizing latent representations learned from real textual data can lead to more effective AI systems that effectively manage complex communication tasks.  This study proposes LEATHER, a computational framework that integrates learning from both simulated dialogues and targeted tasks, using past experiences to enhance its overall performance and communication skills.  By employing LEATHER, we generated highly realistic dialogues that effectively conveyed human emotional states and exhibited consistent emotional responses throughout our evaluation tasks, both with human evaluators and through a controlled simulation of a virtual assistant's behavior.  Our model's effectiveness was evident in its ability to successfully navigate dialogue tasks and maintain consistent emotional responses over time, using past dialogues to inform its performance and maintain a dynamic understanding of human emotions.

This talk will introduce some key techniques for performing lattice QCD simulations at non-zero temperature and density, with a focus on their underlying principles rather than specific applications. An alternative approach for achieving real-time simulations at non-zero density will also be discussed.

A more accurate understanding and design of offshore wind turbines can be gained by conducting full-scale field tests, yet these tests are extremely expensive. To mitigate the costs, data from these tests can be leveraged to develop a comprehensive model of turbine behavior across various wind speeds, temperatures, and wave heights, enabling future turbines to be designed with greater precision. To facilitate this process, we present a new approach using Gaussian processes to create a model of turbine data from an existing field test. Gaussian processes, being non-parametric regression methods, naturally accommodate uncertainty. We further enhance their applicability by developing a technique to chain multiple Gaussian process models together, which significantly reduces uncertainty. To evaluate our approach, we compare the results to established statistical methods for time-series regression, demonstrating our method's superiority in several critical aspects.

Twitter has emerged as a valuable platform for disseminating and analyzing real-time information, particularly in times of crisis such as natural disasters. The ability to pinpoint the origin and track the evolution of events in real-time makes it a crucial communication tool. This study explores Twitter's capabilities by examining public reactions to the 7.5-magnitude earthquake that struck off the coast of Izmir, Turkey, in 2020. By analyzing tweets, we aim to identify the most active periods, affected regions, and categorize the nature of these events. Our analysis leverages the power of machine learning for automatic text classification and the geotag feature of Twitter to pinpoint the epicenter's coordinates. Furthermore, we propose a novel visualization technique, a scatter plot, designed to track and understand event evolution over time.

A group $G$ is termed $R_\infty$ if, for every isomorphic copy of $G$ within another group $H$, the infinite conjugacy classes of $H$ automatically include those of $G$. In a 1991 study by Klyachko, an algorithm was proposed to determine if a finite nilpotent group possesses the $R_\infty$ characteristic. Utilizing this algorithm in 2019, Huang and Li established the $R_\infty$ characteristic for solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups in all but a specific case. Leveraging updated computations, this investigation rectifies that error and explores the $R_\infty$ characteristic of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups under various circumstances.

A data-driven approach, leveraging optimization theory, reconstructs complex physical behaviors from observational data that may be incomplete or inaccurate, focusing on real-world applications, such as reconstructing fluid dynamics from new experimental setups and predicting fluid dynamics from numerical simulations. The proposed method, capable of incorporating prior knowledge efficiently, accurately reconstructs intricate behaviors without adjusting parameters, demonstrating superior stability and precision. The algorithm's versatility is highlighted through successful applications to challenging reconstruction problems.

Naturalistic driving datasets are crucial for understanding real-world driving behaviors. This paper introduces a comprehensive dataset called SceNDD, which captures various real-world driving scenarios captured by instruments on the dashboard. These scenarios capture diverse driving behaviors from hundreds of drivers of different age groups and gender, across various types of vehicles. SCENDD includes situational data, such as critical decision points, along with corresponding sensor data, such as GPS location, G-sensor readings, speed, steering angle, and more. Additionally, the dataset features audio recordings, facial expressions of the driver, and detailed information about the interior and exterior appearance of the vehicle. A pre-processing method is also presented to segment the raw data into reusable scenarios along with essential safety metrics. Lastly, the paper demonstrates the applicability of the dataset in three distinct applications.

In the context of boundary conformal field theory, we explore an "reflected" version of the central charge $c$, entropic central charge $s$, and $c$-central charge $c_T$. This reflected version of the central charge has interesting properties when the defect is a mirror, effectively doubling the reflected entropy in this specific case. Furthermore, when the defect acts as a perfect disconnector, the reflected central entropy demonstrates its ability to serve as a measure of phase transitions in terms of its monotonic decrease with the order parameter.

Extramodular Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a highly adaptable component in future wireless networks, functioning as intermediaries between transmitter and receiver to enhance signal transmission efficiency. In practical settings, the precision of channel estimation algorithms heavily influences RIS performance, particularly in real-world scenarios plagued by hardware flaws and varying channel conditions. To address this issue, we investigate an Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) system with a programmable RIS, incorporating both types of hardware imperfections and uneven channel distributions. Our approach employs an enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (eELM) model, specifically tailored to the channel by integrating prior channel knowledge within the feature matrix, thereby improving channel estimation capabilities. Simulation results demonstrate substantial enhancements in estimation accuracy when compared to Baseline Channel Estimation (BCE) and Minimum Error Mean Square Error (MSE) methods under various hardware flaws and uneven channel distributions, particularly a 0.09 improvement in Mean Square Error (MSE) when both hardware imperfections are present.

This work examines the validity of certain thermodynamic principles under specific conditions of isotropic thermal measurements and constant energy, demonstrating its applicability to systems undergoing arbitrary changes and leaky channels. We investigate scenarios where energy is obtained from the system at a single energy level, revealing deviations from standard results, including FT validity and modified forms of Jarzynski's equation and Crooks theory. We demonstrate that FT remains valid in these scenarios, albeit in a path-dependent form, which may exhibit non-physical behavior, including negative entropy production. Additionally, we explore the implications for work-related statistics, highlighting their non-conservative nature and the inability to infer distribution behavior without assuming isothermal conditions. A notable finding of this study is that work distributions inferred from forward and reverse processes are not identical, resulting in biased probability distributions. We propose a novel method for estimating the free energy difference of a system, utilizing forward and reverse distributions, which remains consistent with the fundamental principle of free energy being greater than or equal to the work done on a system, provided the system's heat is not lost during the process.

We are examining the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. The linearization of the G2-instanton equation results in a second-order elliptic operator acting on 2-forms. This operator is decomposed into irreducible components as part of a new decomposition of the 2-form representation of the G2-group. The decomposition of the deformation complex of a nearly G2-manifold is also presented. The deformation complex of an instanton is related to the linearization of the Einstein equation when the nearly G2-manifold represents a gradient nearly Kähler metric. A review of the geometry of nearly G2-manifolds is also conducted.

This study examines how effectively the Italian app COVID-19, known as CoronavirussUS, protects user privacy within its proximity tracing system. We assess the app's ability to conceal user locations by formulating a probabilistic model that quantifies the risk of inferring a user's geographic location based on reported proximity data. Our analysis reveals that inferring regional coordinates poses significant privacy risks, yet inferring urban coordinates is less problematic due to Italy's geographical constraints. We also investigate the impact of different proximity report accuracy radii on the regional risk model and find that increasing the radius reduces estimation precision and thus lowers user risk. Furthermore, we identify essential parameters that regional risk depends on and develop two performance metrics - Risk and Likelihood Ratio. These statistics can be computed efficiently and demonstrate that risk is independent of the total number of users within a region. The paper concludes by highlighting the distinctions between CoronavirussUS and GPS-based tracing systems through a comprehensive comparison table.

Recently, there has been significant interest in applying quantum machine learning to solve problems that exceed the computational capabilities of classical machines. Our approach involves using quantum circuits to encode data inputs, allowing us to explore quantum advantages. Interestingly, this method of encoding data can be seen as a specific application of traditional neural networks, where classical layers are replaced by quantum circuits. By utilizing this analogy, we can develop more efficient quantum circuits through the knowledge gained from these synthetic layers. Our experiments support our findings that quantum circuits can provide computational advantages and reveal their benefits.

This research introduces a novel tool for automatically generating C code, verified by the ACL2 theorem prover. The 200-page extended version of the research presents enhancements to our prior work, featuring a more advanced C language representation within ACL2 and the inclusion of additional C standard library functions with accompanying ACL2 definitions that facilitate proof-generating C code creation. The library includes definitions for core data types such as arrays, pointers, strings, and basic math functions. The research also demonstrates the feasibility of creating a simpler C language representation to ensure the tool runs quickly, despite encompassing a wide range of C features.

Our study focuses on the dynamics of the (39991) Iochroma family, a cluster that shares specific J2 resonances with Jupiter. Despite extensive numerical integration of Iochroma's J3J4 resonances, Iochmur Iochroma's J2 Jupiter resonances have never been studied. Our work provides a comprehensive overview of the family, examining the effects of Iochroma's J2 resonances with Jupiter and Iochroma's evolution over time. Our analysis indicates that the Iochroma family is not isolated due to inter-cluster collisions. Iochroma lies near the Icheron and Iphidrome groups, and we found that inter-cluster J2-Jupiter resonances dominate over collisional effects within Iochroma, leading to a significant impact on the family's dynamics. Our study also identified Iochroma's I10 member, 2002 TC302, which exhibits Iochroma-like features.

Building upon the harmonic series, the Hurwitz Zeta function generalizes it. Ramanujan established a striking result regarding this series, which we will generalize further, revealing that certain expressions involving products and derivatives of the Hurwitz Zeta function yield both $\zeta'(0)$ and $\zeta'(1)$, a fact that aligns with the spirit of Ramanujan's theorem. We will provide explicit formulas for these expressions at arbitrary depth and order, accompanied by numerous illustrative examples and numerous novel identities.

This article demonstrates that logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the complex projective space CP(V) is isomorphic to a module consisting of a circle-equivariant difference equation solutions, specifically in the variable z. A specific consideration is given to the case where V takes the form V=V_2 and the level-1 elliptic cohomology of CP(V) is found to be isomorphic to the circle-equivariant cohomology of the space V itself. This particular case of elliptic echelon cohomology serves as a novel topological order parameter in the study of elliptic Chern-Simons theory.

We've developed a physics-informed machine learning approach for discovering novel algebraic topological models in the field of quantum many-body systems, specifically in spin chains governed by local Hamiltonians with a topological index known as the string-dyad invariant, $\nu_{SD}$. We've found that by incorporating physical laws into the training process, we can achieve better results in identifying complex Hamiltonians and achieving accurate classifications of $\nu_{SD}$. Moreover, our neural network has been able to uncover an overlooked scenario involving a $\mathbb{Z}_3$-protected string chain and we've identified an analytical expression defining this state in terms of correlations, thus expanding our understanding of these systems beyond binary classifications.

This research undertones a comprehensive, to the best of current knowledge, next-to-leading-order (NLO) analysis of the $J/\psi$ angular distributions in the processes $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ at the Belle and BaBar energy range of $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. Calculations are carried out within the nonrelativistic quantum chromodynamics (NRQCD) factorization framework. Numerical outcomes are presented with and without color octet contributions, and comparisons with the available experimental data are discussed.

This study examines the understanding of Signal's end-to-end encrypted messaging app user personas and their selection of cryptographic secrets. A research paper resulting from a survey of 50 Signal users reveals that many users lack awareness of the app's privacy features and the function of its cryptographic secrets. Consequently, the research suggests promoting Signal's security and privacy principles to encourage users to prioritize these features when setting up their accounts.

In autonomous solar energy systems with battery storage, solar energy stored in the battery under conditions x over the time interval [t1, t2] is crucial to determine the optimal control strategy. Researchers typically rely on measurements from two key indicators: net solar energy storage and power grid connection. However, directly utilizing this continuous solar energy information proves challenging due to its high dimensionality. To streamline decision-making, an innovative approach called solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature is proposed to condense solar energy into a manageable set of state variables, leveraging a limited number of key time points determined by local weather patterns and geography. The proposed method was successfully applied to a real-world setting, achieving high precision with approximately 10% overhead in storage capacity under specific solar-weighted integration.

The performance of first-order optimization methods like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can be significantly improved by incorporating second-order information, but storing the full curvature of the loss function is impractical. Our proposed method, ViViT, utilizes a sparsified version of the generalized Newton matrix to efficiently approximate this curvature. ViViT achieves this by introducing variable inner radii in the curvature dimension, effectively adapting the dimension's influence on the optimization process. Our experiments demonstrate that ViViT outperforms state-of-the-art second-order methods like SAGAN, SGBDt, and SPIDER3, while surpassing gradient descent methods such as SGD, SVRG, and PROX-SVRG, all of which utilize first-order information.

We examine the impact of grammatical gender on semantic gender - distinct from biological gender - within languages that have gendered nouns. To achieve this, we employ a cross-linguistic analysis of Czech, incorporating both a dataset of Czech nouns categorized by grammatical gender and semantic gender, and comparative analysis with English, a language lacking grammatical gender marking. Our investigation utilizes machine learning-based similarity assessments to gauge semantic gender effects in Czech representations, discovering notable gender-based similarities that align with existing research findings. Additionally, we develop a method to pinpoint individual gender associations in Czech through our 'Association Strength Distribution' approach, ultimately confirming that these links can be accurately reconstructed.

We introduce the problem of Zero-Sapose, which entails inferring 3D object pose
categories at a coarse level from a single image. This prediction can then be
utilized for subsequent tasks, such as refining the class-level object pose and
addressing further applications. This task poses a significant challenge due to
the lack of annotated class-level pose data and the absence of reliable pose
predictions from state-of-the-art methods. To address this issue, we develop a
multi-task framework that learns to predict object poses and categories
simultaneously. This framework incorporates a segmentation-based loss for object
localization, as well as a novel classification loss based on re-weighted class
frequencies. When applied to real-world data, our method outperforms previous
approaches in both simulated and real-world settings and excels at out-of-distribution
class-level pose prediction. Furthermore, our method excels in semantic
segmentation, where it achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

Traffic forecast models are crucial for optimizing transportation systems, but they are typically limited to network sections with extensive data coverage, which is not always available. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that can handle sections with sparse data by using a data-driven method to extract key features. This approach involves identifying and incorporating information from similar areas within the same city or even other cities. The proposed method has been tested on a large-scale dataset and has shown significant improvements in forecast accuracy for network sections with moderate to very limited data coverage.

In the realm of causal inference, a fundamental challenge lies in estimating a causal graph's effects when certain causal relationships are absent from the data. Existing VGA algorithms excel in predicting interventional questions under specific causal mismatches, yet fall short in addressing partial natural settings and predicting counterfactual inquiries. Our enhanced VGA algorithms successfully tackle these issues, yielding improved counterfactual QE estimates compared to prior counterfactual estimators in simulated data. Moreover, in real-world data concerning hospital admissions due to COVID-19, our approach yields more accurate results for both interventional and counterfactual questions under various causal mismatches.

Transients in radio astronomy, characterized by short, intense bursts of energy, are a topic of ongoing interest due to their unique properties and the diverse phenomena that may produce them. To identify and study these events efficiently, we need a reliable method for flagging transients in real-time. At the Irish LOFAR station, we've implemented an advanced system called REALTA, capable of pinpointing transients at 330 MHz in real-time. By examining one month of data from July 1, 2021, we've identified 12 events that match our criteria, including 11 distinct and one overlapping event. Our analysis reveals that the transients we've discovered behave similarly to previously found radio bursts in this frequency range.

A thorough examination of recent developments in metaphotonics is presented, encompassing cutting-edge methodologies for the fabrication of metaphotonically enhanced devices. Research in this area boasts the remarkable achievement of achieving exceptionally swift, highly accurate, and reliable sensing capabilities utilizing cutting-edge metaphotonics-based structures. By integrating cutting-edge machine intelligence, metaphorotonics has been propelled to new heights in achieving cutting-edge performance metrics. A comprehensive analysis of metaphorotonics research, including cutting-edge structures, fabrication techniques, and machine intelligence integration, has motivated the development of state-of-the-art structures, as well as a machine learning-based method to expedite the design process. These structures exhibit exceptional performance in areas such as sensing, switching, modulation, and multiplexing. Furthermore, a machine learning algorithm has been employed to significantly expedite the design process associated with these structures.

The film industry's high-risk nature has long been a topic of interest to researchers, driven by the difficulty studios face in predicting a film's success before production. This challenge stems from the inherent asymmetry of information, where films already in production have some known attributes, while upcoming films lack these insights. Past research primarily examined the impact of known film characteristics on revenue potential using linear regression models, overlooking crucial aspects like individual film production costs, which are crucial to understanding a film's return on investment. This research addresses these gaps by compiling a comprehensive database of over 4300 films from 1991 to 2018, which are analyzed using a non-linear Bayesian model to account for the goal of maximizing return on investment. Furthermore, we incorporate each film's production cost into our analysis and employ a quantile regression model to investigate the influence of pre-release information on revenue potential, ultimately demonstrating the importance of our approach by revealing the return on investment's correlation with a film's popularity, independent of its box office revenue.

This work examines the integration of frequency regulation into a network of voltage machines, which are derived from simplifying the dynamics of large power stations. As the mode frequencies associated with frequency machines are typically lower than those of the network, their inclusion tends to dampen voltage oscillations, thereby improving overall system stability, even in networks that were previously unstable. Furthermore, certain preparatory steps can be taken to ensure that frequency machines contribute auxiliary support to the network's stability through frequency control design. Notably, this effect remains robust under diverse operating conditions, and it holds for a broader class of voltage machines beyond those considered here.

The integration of computing, communication, and electronic systems into physical entities has given rise to a new category of systems, known as cyber-physical systems (CPS). The interconnection of these individual CPS through networks, known as networks of networks (NoN), is now widely used to execute a broad range of functions, such as controlling critical infrastructure and managing transportation networks. However, the inherent limitations of traditional NoN designs have given rise to the need for incorporating artificial intelligence and machine learning capabilities, to enable adaptive learning and intelligence within these networks. This evolution will facilitate the development of more resilient and robust NoN structures capable of withstanding disruptions and malfunctions while maintaining operational efficiency and stability under adverse conditions.

Blazars are a subset of active galactic nuclei characterized by highly polarized electromagnetic radiation resulting from the interaction of relativistic particles within their jets with surrounding photon fields, such as optical/UV radiation from the host galaxy, and orbital electrons in the case of X-ray emissions. A significant factor contributing to the polarization of emitted radiation is magnetic field disorder within the blazar jet, necessitating a practical approach to modeling this disorder. We developed MAPPIES, a Monte-Carlo code designed to simulate Compton scattering of external photons by relativistic electrons under the influence of disordered magnetic fields. MAPPIES incorporates a Gaussian random magnetic field model, enabling us to investigate the effects of intrinsic blazar jet magnetization on observed emission properties, including spectral energy distributions and polarization fractions. Our results reveal that significant UV/soft X-ray excess polarization is unlikely, but rather that polarization is reduced, consistent with the presence of relativistic electrons interacting with optical/UV radiation within the host galaxy. Furthermore, MAPPIES enables us to derive the required magnetic field strength and size for various blazars, including Mrk 421, Mrk 501, and BL Lac, and to assess the feasibility of measuring polarization in other blazar sources, such as PKS 2121-332, using the CTA Cherenkov Telescope Array.

A new method has been developed to map atmospheric parameters across star-forming galactic central regions, leveraging the spatial correlation between emission lines at different frequencies. This method employs a statistical approach based on a linear relationship, allowing the analysis of multiple frequency pairs simultaneously through Monte Carlo simulations. To test this method's effectiveness, it was applied to two young star clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud, specifically R140 and R142. The technique was able to produce maps at all frequency pairs analyzed, including radio and submillimeter wavelengths. The resulting electron temperature maps, along with electron density maps, align with the predictions of recombination theory, and the observed variations in temperature across the star clusters, along with their associated uncertainties, were determined.

In quantum mechanics, identical particles of the same type have the property that swapping two particles results in either a phase factor of +1 or -1.  This property is known as fermionic (+1) or bosonic (-1) behavior.  Although it's straightforward to identify a purely bosonic state, creating a fermionic state that's in a single, definable condition (a pure state) is extremely challenging.  In fact, it's been suggested that it might not be feasible.  This paper outlines a method for verifying that a pure state of N particles is indeed a fermionic state, along with an explanation of a corresponding protocol that can accomplish this verification.  This protocol can operate using a technique known as quantum homomorphic evaluation, which allows the computation of a function without the need to measure the input.  By applying this method, the paper demonstrates that it's possible to confirm a pure fermionic state, even in its most basic (pure) condition.  Moreover, the paper assesses a wide range of typical states and finds that our approach can effectively distinguish between them.  As a result, it's possible to confirm that these states are not fermionic without the need to change them.  This discovery has significant implications for the field of quantum information and for the development of advanced technologies such as topological quantum computers.

Baryon creation can be explained by the dynamics of a quantized filament exhibiting helical patterns, which forms a key component of a proposed model for baryogenesis. This model draws inspiration from a filament previously introduced as a model for meson production, which successfully captured the dynamics of a meson through coherent states of the filament. In the present work, we present a first-principles approach to the baryon dynamics based on the fragmentation of a quantized filament with quantized levels of helical coiling. We discuss baryon production in the context of the quantized filament model and compare it to the previously studied meson production model, as well as to the standard Weinberg model for baryon generation.

The sun's surface exhibits a distinct travel-time pattern, characterized by faster movements along its equator and slower along its poles. Researchers believe this phenomenon is driven by horizontal movements within the solar atmosphere, possibly associated with large-scale surface features. To investigate this, we conducted high-resolution simulations on a spherical simulator, modeling the sun's outer layer. By analyzing our 3D simulations, we calculated the travel-time patterns and compared them to actual sun observations, focusing specifically on the travel-time patterns around active areas. Our study reveals that active areas significantly contribute to the observed travel-time patterns, primarily through their associated large-scale surface features.

Inflationary models typically produce only vector curvature perturbations, not tensor ones, which means they don't generate $\text{B}$-mode polarization in the Cosmic Microwave Background or create gravitational waves detectable in the LIGO band. To explore another possibility, this work investigates whether primordial electromagnetic fields can create a gravitational signal. It's found that if a strong primordial electromagnetic background exists, it will induce linear tensor perturbations. For a given curvature perturbation amplitude, stronger initial electromagnetic fields result in larger tensor modes. It's estimated that tensor modes at the time of the Planck epoch could have exceeded the curvature perturbations, and these modes would reside within the Pulsar Timing Array frequency band today.

A new, lightweight, low-resolution, and rate-efficient compression method for light field images is developed, leveraging 3D Conventional Neural Networks, where low-resolution sub-aperture images are utilized as an auxiliary input, allowing the implicit reconstruction of actual LF images through learned mapping relationships. Due to the inherent redundancy among these input images and the explicit mapping, the encoding process is significantly reduced. Moreover, by integrating the input images with disparity information, the proposed approach effectively enhances the visual quality of the decoded LF images, especially with respect to moiré effects. Through comprehensive evaluations conducted on multiple datasets, our proposed method achieves notable improvements over prevailing alternatives in both efficiency and visual quality metrics.

Current multilingual corpora are scarce, limiting the effectiveness of cross-lingual information retrieval. To address this challenge, interactive retrieval has been proposed, which capitalizes on users' ability to provide additional context for query refinement through iterated interactions. However, interactive sessions can be time-consuming and impractical in certain applications, such as those involving web searches requiring rapid response times. This research aims to bridge the gap between interactive and non-interactive frameworks, achieving comparable performance under both settings. Furthermore, insights gained from enhancing non-interactive performance can inform future cross-lingual models developed by leveraging human assistance during interactive sessions.

Design-based techniques were employed to estimate area-specific HIV prevalence rates in Uganda, a country with limited resources. A total of 1,096 Ugandan communities were stratified into urban and rural areas, with 200, 1,096 individuals tested for HIV. A unique aspect of this study was the application of various design-based approaches to calculate low-area prevalence rates. Additionally, a few model-based methods, including Bayesian small-area estimation techniques, were used to estimate the prevalence rates. Models used included logistic and probit models, as well as small-area empirical Bayesian estimation, with results from all approaches being presented. A surprising outcome was the lack of significant differences between the various approaches used to estimate area-specific HIV prevalence rates in Uganda.

This study explores the application of classical Wagering theory, specifically the Kelly Wagering formula, within the realm of Quantum Wagering. By leveraging continuous variable quantum systems, we model wagering scenarios that can be mapped out using the fundamental principles of Quantum Wagering. Building upon the principles of quantum probability theory, as defined by Qubics, we represent wagering scenarios using quantum stochastic processes and update wagering strategies using Quantum Wagering formulae expressed in Qubics-qubits. Our theoretical framework, specifically the law of large numbers for quantum systems, enables us to verify the validity of our Quantum Wagering formulae.

This study investigates the two-dimensional semiconductors consisting of group 6 metals, group 14 semiconductors and a group 15 element, specifically $\text{Mo}_2$ $\text{Si}_4$ $\text{N}_8$ and $\text{W}_2$ $\text{Si}_4$ $\text{P}_8$. We demonstrate that $\text{Mo}_2$ $\text{Si}_4$ $\text{N}_8$ and $\text{W}_2$ $\text{Si}_4$ $\text{P}_8$ have a unique quasiparticle band arrangement, with a large number of excitonic states located just below the conduction continuum. We further explore the effects of replacing phosphorus with germanium and compare the resulting structures with $\text{Mo}_2$ $\text{Ge}_4$ $\text{N}_8$ and $\text{W}_2$ $\text{Ge}_4$ $\text{P}_8$. Notably, $\text{Mo}_2$ $\text{Ge}_4$ $\text{N}_8$ and $\text{W}_2$ $\text{Ge}_4$ $\text{P}_8$ exhibit stacking independence and a similar quasiparticle band arrangement, with a larger bandgap and fewer quasiparticle states, contrasting the behaviors of $\text{Mo}_2$ $\text{Si}_4$ $\text{

The transition from a Sigma-plus to a proton accompanied by a muon pair has been observed for the first time, proving that this process involving flavor-changing neutral currents and lepton pair production can occur. This investigation has provided the necessary conditions to analyze the underlying physics mechanisms governing such a reaction at the Large Hadron Collider. Specifically, researchers have relied heavily on form factors to evaluate the Standard Model's predictions for this process. Furthermore, their analysis has yielded an upper limit for the rate of this reaction of $1.3 \times 10^{-4}$ based on the data collected in 2011.

The origin of planetary systems is traced back to the collapse of pre-stellar cores, which have flat structures that may lead to protoplanetary disk formation.
Using the experiment of a 0.1 solar mass core, which resulted in a protoplanetary disk, we conducted a numerical study to understand the formation of these disks.
Our calculations showed that a pre-stellar core's collapse leads to a protoplanetary disk forming due to angular momentum conservation, which is consistent with current observations of planetary disk shapes.
However, the central star's heat emission is insufficient to vaporize the gas in the disk, which poses a challenge to planet formation.
Nonetheless, if the core has a higher mass, which results in a higher mass star, the resulting heat will be sufficient to vaporize the disk gas, allowing planets to form within it.

The observed variability in brightness of white dwarf stars is widely believed to be a result of their circumstellar dust atmospheres, yet it remains unclear how their mass and composition impact observed fluctuations. Our research involved analyzing the spectra of variable white dwarf stars, specifically those with masses around 0.6 solar masses, in order to gain a better understanding of how their atmospheric properties affect their variability patterns. By comparing the spectra of a particular star, known as the Type 1904, taken at different times, we discovered that its atmosphere undergoes significant changes in both the near-infrared and optical regions. Our models suggest that its mass remains relatively stable, yet its composition changes significantly, indicating that its growth in mass occurs in the near-infrared region. By combining optical and near-infrared observations, our research has allowed us to refine the characterization of these variable white dwarf atmospheres, in particular those with masses around 0.6 solar masses, and has shown that their variability patterns are influenced by their atmospheric properties. By combining the results of our research with other observations, we have been able to narrow down the possible range of their mass and composition, in particular those with masses around 0.6 solar masses, and have found that their variability patterns are influenced by their atmospheric properties.
